concepts.name: PMJDY: Core Architecture and Launch Context
key_dimensions: Launched on August 28, 2014 — National Mission on Financial Inclusion; distinction from earlier schemes like No-Frills Accounts
Three pillars: Banking the unbanked, Securing the unsecured, Funding the unfunded — trap: UPSC may test which pillar covers which benefit
Shift from household-based to individual-based account opening — significance for women's financial autonomy
Replacing No-Frills Accounts vs. upgrading them — common confusion area

concepts.name: Zero-Balance Account Feature and Its Limitations
key_dimensions: PMJDY accounts can be opened with zero balance — but interest is earned (trap: students assume no interest)
Minimum balance requirement is NIL, yet overdraft facility requires satisfactory account operation for 6 months — sequence dependency
Distinction between Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA) and PMJDY account — both allow zero balance but differ in transaction limits
Recent controversy: Dormant/inoperative accounts reducing effective financial inclusion metrics

concepts.name: Overdraft (OD) Facility under PMJDY
key_dimensions: OD limit revised from ₹5,000 to ₹10,000 in 2018 — and further nuances: ₹2,000 without conditions, beyond that with conditions
Eligibility: Account must be operational for 6 months; preference to women account holders — UPSC trap on gender preference clause
Age eligibility: 18–65 years for OD — trap: general account opening has no such restriction
OD is NOT a loan but a credit facility — distinction matters for questions on credit access vs. formal lending

concepts.name: RuPay Debit Card and Accidental Insurance Cover
key_dimensions: Every PMJDY account holder gets RuPay Debit Card with accidental insurance of ₹2 lakh (revised from ₹1 lakh in 2018) — trap: old vs. new figures
Condition: Card must be used at least once in 90 days prior to accident for insurance claim — a critical operational condition often missed
Life cover of ₹30,000 for accounts opened between Aug 2014–Jan 2015 only — trap: this is NOT available to all account holders
RuPay card as domestic payments infrastructure — link to Digital India and reducing dependence on Visa/Mastercard

concepts.name: Financial Inclusion vs. Financial Deepening — Conceptual Distinction
key_dimensions: Financial inclusion = access; Financial deepening = usage — PMJDY addresses access but deepening remains a challenge
Metrics: Account ownership (access) vs. frequency of transactions (deepening) vs. credit penetration (deepening)
PMJDY success on inclusion metrics but criticism on dormant accounts — policy trap: high numbers ≠ high impact
Comparison with Global Findex Database findings on India's inclusion trajectory post-2014

concepts.name: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) and PMJDY Linkage
key_dimensions: PMJDY accounts as the terminal point of DBT ecosystem — JAM Trinity: Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile
Leakage reduction in welfare schemes (LPG subsidy, MGNREGS wages, PM-KISAN) — quantifiable impact area
Aadhaar-seeding of PMJDY accounts as mandatory vs. voluntary — Supreme Court judgment on Aadhaar (2018) nuance
COVID-19 ex-gratia transfers to women Jan Dhan accounts — live example of DBT utility

concepts.name: JAM Trinity: Integration, Mechanism and Gaps
key_dimensions: Jan Dhan (account) + Aadhaar (identity) + Mobile (interface) — each component's role and interdependency
Gaps: Mobile penetration in rural areas, Aadhaar authentication failures (exclusion errors), last-mile banking connectivity
JAM as a financial infrastructure vs. JAM as a welfare delivery mechanism — dual role distinction
Economic Survey 2016-17 coined JAM — attribution and policy context important for Prelims

concepts.name: Business Correspondent (BC) Model and Last-Mile Delivery
key_dimensions: BCs act as agents of banks — they are NOT bank employees; regulated by RBI guidelines
BC model as solution to branch viability in remote areas — cost vs. reach trade-off
Challenges: BC dropout rates, technology failures, fraudulent transactions at BC points — policy gap area
Distinction: BC (individual agent) vs. BF (Business Facilitator) — BF only facilitates, BC actually conducts transactions

concepts.name: Gender Dimension of PMJDY: Women's Financial Inclusion
key_dimensions: Over 55% of PMJDY accounts held by women (as of recent data) — significance for women's economic empowerment
Preference for women in OD facility — explicit policy design for gender equity
Link to SHG-bank linkage programme and NRLM — convergence of schemes
Distinction: Account ownership ≠ account control — women may hold accounts but men may control funds (agency problem)

concepts.name: PMJDY vs. Earlier Financial Inclusion Schemes
key_dimensions: No-Frills Accounts (2005) → BSBDA (2012) → PMJDY (2014) — evolutionary trajectory, not replacement in all cases
BSBDA features vs. PMJDY features — BSBDA has transaction limits (4 per month); PMJDY does not impose such strict limits
Swabhimaan Campaign (2011) vs. PMJDY — coverage approach (village-level vs. household-level)
PMJDY's innovation: Insurance + OD + RuPay card as bundled product — distinguishes it from predecessors

concepts.name: Dormant Accounts Problem and Effective Financial Inclusion
key_dimensions: High percentage of zero-balance/dormant accounts challenges the 'success' narrative — critical analysis dimension
Definition of dormant account: No transaction for 2 years — RBI norms applicable
Policy responses: DBT linkage to activate accounts, financial literacy campaigns, incentivizing BCs
Trap: UPSC may ask whether dormant accounts indicate failure of PMJDY — nuanced answer required (access achieved, usage pending)

concepts.name: Micro-Insurance and Pension Schemes Linked to PMJDY Ecosystem
key_dimensions: PMJDY is the gateway for Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), and Atal Pension Yojana (APY)
Premium auto-debit from Jan Dhan accounts — operational linkage
PMSBY: ₹2 lakh accidental cover at ₹20/year; PMJJBY: ₹2 lakh life cover at ₹436/year — figures trap
Distinction: RuPay card insurance (free, accidental) vs. PMSBY (paid, accidental) vs. PMJJBY (paid, life) — three different instruments, common confusion

concepts.name: Financial Literacy as a Prerequisite for Financial Inclusion
key_dimensions: PMJDY without financial literacy = 'bank account but no banking behavior' — structural limitation
National Strategy for Financial Education (NSFE) 2020-2025 — RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA joint initiative
Centre for Financial Literacy (CFL) programme under RBI — block-level financial literacy
Trap: Financial literacy is a demand-side intervention; BC model is supply-side — UPSC may ask about supply vs. demand side barriers

concepts.name: RBI's Role vs. Government's Role in Financial Inclusion
key_dimensions: RBI mandates: Priority Sector Lending (PSL), BC guidelines, BSBDA norms — regulatory role
Government mandates: PMJDY implementation, DBT, subsidy architecture — executive role
Overlap area: Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks — RBI licensed them for inclusion; Government uses them for DBT
Trap: NABARD (rural credit) vs. RBI (regulation) vs. Government (scheme implementation) — three-way distinction in financial inclusion ecosystem

concepts.name: Payment Banks and Small Finance Banks: Inclusion Architecture
key_dimensions: Payment Banks: Cannot lend, can accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh, focus on remittances — trap: they CANNOT give loans
Small Finance Banks: Can lend (primarily to small borrowers), full banking license — distinction from Payment Banks
Both licensed by RBI under Nachiket Mor Committee recommendations (2014) — policy genesis
India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) as largest Payment Bank — postal network as last-mile connector for PMJDY

concepts.name: Credit Exclusion Despite Account Inclusion — The Missing Middle
key_dimensions: Having a bank account ≠ access to formal credit — PMJDY addresses deposits, not credit access
Informal moneylenders persist despite PMJDY — demand for credit remains unmet for small borrowers
Mudra Yojana (PMMY) as the credit complement to PMJDY — Shishu, Kishor, Tarun categories
Trap: PMJDY OD facility (₹10,000) is NOT sufficient for productive credit needs — limits of the scheme

concepts.name: Interoperability and Digital Payments Ecosystem Post-PMJDY
key_dimensions: PMJDY + UPI (Unified Payments Interface) linkage — Jan Dhan accounts can be linked to UPI for digital transactions
NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) as the backbone — operates RuPay, UPI, NACH (for DBT auto-credit)
Trap: NPCI is NOT a government body — it is a not-for-profit company promoted by RBI and Indian Banks Association
Interoperability between Jan Dhan accounts across banks via IMPS/UPI — reduces dependency on specific bank branches

concepts.name: Measuring Financial Inclusion: Indices and Indicators
key_dimensions: RBI's Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index): Launched 2021, composite of Access + Usage + Quality — annual publication, no base year
Global Findex Database (World Bank): Compares account ownership globally — India's improvement post-PMJDY documented here
Distinction: FI-Index measures inclusion comprehensively; PMJDY metrics only measure account opening — scope difference
Trap: High FI-Index score does not mean poverty reduction — inclusion is necessary but not sufficient condition

concepts.name: PMJDY and Federalism: Centre-State Implementation Dynamics
key_dimensions: PMJDY is a centrally sponsored mission but implementation relies on public sector banks, RRBs, and cooperative banks — multi-institutional
Regional Rural Banks (RRBs): Sponsored by scheduled commercial banks, supervised by NABARD — role in rural PMJDY implementation
State-level variation in financial inclusion outcomes — North-East states had lower banking penetration; special focus districts identified
Trap: PMJDY is NOT a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) in the traditional sense — it is a national mission implemented through banks, not through state governments

concepts.name: Financial Inclusion and Poverty Reduction: Causal vs. Correlational Link
key_dimensions: Having a bank account reduces transaction costs of receiving welfare, but does not directly reduce poverty — causality trap
Evidence: PMJDY + DBT reduced LPG subsidy leakage by ₹1.4 lakh crore (government claim) — but attribution debate exists
Financial inclusion as enabler of other SDGs (SDG 1: No Poverty, SDG 5: Gender Equality, SDG 8: Decent Work) — multidimensional linkage
Criticism: Without accompanying credit, insurance, and income generation, bank accounts alone are insufficient — Amartya Sen's capabilities approach relevance
